history.text: Hey makers, what's the most important thing you cut from your MVP to get it out the door?

slots.brief: A playful, debatable opinion about coding from a laptop versus a phone, remote terminal, or server. Make it personal opinion, not a claim that beginners are inferior.
A playful opinion about terminal tools, editor extensions and knowing when to stop configuring.
Invite solo founders working after their day job to compare notes.
Ask what founders would validate before spending a weekend building again.
Ask what feedback made someone change their product rather than add another feature.
A playful contrast between a polished landing page and an unfinished core workflow.
A debatable opinion about boring dependable software versus rewriting everything with a new framework.
Invite a one-sentence product description and who it helps. Make trying it conditional on a real need.
Invite a scrappy useful prototype that works even though its design is unfinished.
Invite a small open-source side project and the problem it solves. Do not promise to star or promote it.
An opinion about reading the diff before trusting an AI coding assistant.
A short witty observation about spending longer choosing a stack than shipping a feature.
Ask which small user experience improvement mattered more than a big new feature.
Ask builders what they cut from an MVP to actually ship it.
Greet early-stage founders and invite a conversation about building before everything looks polished.
Greet builders still at their first user and invite an honest conversation without revenue flexes.
Invite technical and nontechnical cofounders to discuss the hardest handoff in building together.
Ask for a tool that removes one annoying repetitive task, plus the task it removes.
A brief relatable joke about debugging a tiny bug that turned out to be a wrong assumption.
A witty observation about collecting ideas versus finishing one tiny working product.
